name: Pence as pounds
brief:
A ledger keeps every amount as a whole number of pence. A report shows it in pounds, with commas between thousands, two decimal places and a minus sign before the £ for a loss: `-£1,234.05`. In an f-string, `{n:,}` puts commas between thousands and `{n:02d}` pads a whole number to two digits: `f'{1234567:,}'` is `'1,234,567'` and `f'{5:02d}'` is `'05'`.

Write `format_pence(p)`. `p` is an `int` and can be far larger than a float holds exactly, so work in whole numbers.

Example. `format_pence(-123405)` is `'-£1,234.05'`, and `format_pence(5)` is `'£0.05'`.
constraints: All the tests in a run share one 5-second limit in the browser.
hint: Split off the sign first. Then `abs(p) // 100` is the pounds and `abs(p) % 100` the pence.

examples.note: 1,234 pounds and 5 pence, and the minus sign comes before the £.
Five pence needs a leading zero in the pence.

how: Submit runs 12 hidden tests. Each answer must equal the expected value.
solution:
def format_pence(p):
    sign = '-' if p < 0 else ''
    pounds, pence = divmod(abs(p), 100)
    return f'{sign}£{pounds:,}.{pence:02d}'
notes: `divmod` on the absolute value splits pounds from pence with no rounding at all.
`p / 100` turns a large `int` into a float, which drops the last digits, and a negative `p` formats as `£-12.30`.
The work grows with the number of digits only, so every test is instant.

planted.slip: Formatting `p / 100` directly puts the minus sign after the £.
Dividing by 100 makes a float, which loses pence once `p` passes about $2^{53}$.
